Items.Authors: Gudmundur K. Stefansson, Arpita Roy, Gabor Furesz, Pete Klupar, John DiPalma, Ewan Douglas, Fan Yang Yang, Sander Zandbergen, Stuart Feldman, Saul Perlmutter, Greg Aldering, Patrick Ingraham, Douglas Kelly, S. Pete Worden, Ramya Anche, Nicole Arulanantham, Heejoo Choi, Kevin Derby, Jerry Edelstein, Mike Eiklenborg, Paul Giuliano, Justin Hom, Hyukmo Kang, Daewook Koo, Leander Lacroix, James Lasker, Jared Males, Kian Milani, Timothy N. Miller, Kelsey L. Miller, Pierre Nicolas, Laurent Pueyo, Mickael Rigault, Stephanie Rinaldi, Sanchit Sabhlok, Everett Schlawin, Irina I. Stefan, Saraswathi K. Subramanian, Kyle Van Gorkom, Thomas Wevers, Andre F. Wong, Jaegun Yoo
Items.Title: The Lazuli Space Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Lazuli Space Observatory is a 3m space observatory designed for rapid-response observations and precision astrophysics across optical and near-infrared wavelengths. An off-axis telescope delivers diffraction-limited image quality to three instruments: 1) The Widefield Context Camera (WCC), capable of high-cadence multi-band imaging. 2) The Lazuli Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS), capable of precise spectrophotometry across 400-1700nm at a resolution of R~100-500. 3) The ExtraSolar Coronagraph (ESC), providing high-contrast imaging expected to reach raw contrasts of 1e-8 and post-processed contrasts approaching 1e-9. Operating from a 3:1 lunar-resonant orbit, Lazuli will respond to targets of opportunity in under 4 hours. Lazuli is conceived as a general-purpose facility capable of supporting a wide range of astrophysical investigations with open time for the global community. We describe the observatory architecture and its capabilities in the preliminary design phase.

Items.Authors: Matthew C. H. Leung, David Charbonneau, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, Colby Jurgenson
Items.Title: Optical design of VIPER: a high-resolution multimode fiber-fed VIPA spectrograph for characterizing atmospheric escape
Items.Abstract: Spectrographs based on a Virtually Imaged Phased Array (VIPA) offer a compelling alternative to conventional grating-based spectrographs, providing higher dispersion, higher throughput, and a more compact form factor. We are developing VIPER, a high-resolution, multimode fiber-fed, narrowband, seeing-limited VIPA spectrograph for the 1.5 m Tillinghast Telescope on Mount Hopkins, Arizona, USA. With a resolving power of 300,000 over a 25 nm bandpass, VIPER is specifically designed to probe exoplanet atmospheric escape through the helium 1083 nm triplet line. We present recent progress in developing VIPER’s optical design, with the aim of maximizing throughput and diffraction efficiency. In particular, we discuss the challenges associated with using a multimode fiber, rather than a single mode fiber, to feed a VIPA spectrograph. We validate our resulting design using analytical calculations, simulations in Zemax OpticStudio, and laboratory testing.

Items.Authors: Christopher Madden
Items.Title: Builder of Observatory Behaviors (BOB): an interactive platform for modeling observatory operations
Items.Abstract: BOB: Builder of Observatory Behaviors is a real-time simulation tool built in Unreal Engine 5 to visualize and prototype operational procedures for the Giant Magellan Telescope. Using imported BIM and CAD geometry, BOB provides both an immersive Simulator Mode for interactive exploration and an Editor Mode for constructing and saving “behavior” scenarios. The platform enables observatory personnel to evaluate accessibility, safety, readiness, and efficiency well before construction. By integrating observatory systems into an immersive virtual environment, BOB enhances the development and communication of complex operational concepts.

Items.Authors: Enrico Virgilli, Philippe Laurent
Items.Title: The PHEMTO mission proposal for the M8 ESA Call
Items.Abstract: High-energy observations are essential to understand the behavior of matter around black holes, acceleration processes at shocks linked to cosmic-ray origin, and the non-thermal X-ray content of galaxy clusters. Hard X-ray polarimetry adds a unique diagnostic where non-thermal phenomena dominate, probing acceleration, magnetic fields, and emission mechanisms. The Polarimetric High-Energy Modular Telescope Observatory (PHEMTO), proposed as ESA’s 8th medium mission in “Voyage 2050,” uses a Laue lens and multilayer optics to focus photons onto a Si matrix and CdTe/CZT spectrometer at 20 m. It offers fine spectroscopy and polarimetry over 1–400 keV. This talk will outline PHEMTO’s science goals, technologies, maturity, and mission concept.

Items.Authors: Theodore A. Grosson, Maaike A. M. van Kooten, Kathryn Jackson, Jean-Pierre Veran, Simon Carrier
Items.Title: 96 kHz imaging on an adaptive optics system with a single-photon avalanche diode
Items.Abstract: Astronomical observations requiring extremely high angular resolution necessitate advanced adaptive optics (AO) systems to overcome blurring caused by the atmosphere. In addition to obtaining much sharper point-spread functions (PSFs) with these systems, it is beneficial to be able to characterize the behaviour of the resulting PSF across time and wavelength. We have installed a commercially-available Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) detector on the focal plane of the REVOLT AO testbench, allowing us to observe the visible PSF of the system at rates up to 96 kHz. This provides a time-resolved view of the PSF at ~100 times the frequency of the AO system itself. We use this detector to analyze the high-frequency behaviour of the PSF of the AO system, as well as perform AO-assisted lucky imaging. We compare the PSFs imaged with this detector to other wavelengths and time resolutions to best characterize the performance of REVOLT across wavelengths.

Items.Authors: Candice M. Fazar
Items.Title: A bestiary of low-level electrical artifacts in SPHEREx flight data
Items.Abstract: SPHEREx, NASA’s all-sky spectrophotometric survey mission, maps the sky in 102 spectral channels from 0.75-5 microns at 6.2” resolution from low-Earth orbit using a custom readout of six HAWAII-2RG detectors. The SPHEREx instrument team and Science Data Center have built a robust science data pipeline that includes mitigating image-space artifacts arising from low-level optical and electronic effects. Analysis of first-survey flight data has confirmed predictions for some of these effects, determined differences between the laboratory and flight predictions in others, and even found new artifacts that were unanticipated. This paper will summarize our current understanding of artifacts in SPHEREx images, including image-space artifacts resulting from cosmic rays, crosstalk and unresponsive pixels. We also present mitigation and/or masking strategies implemented to mitigate such effects, and an assessment of the possible implications for other space missions using HAWAII-2RG detectors.

Items.Authors: Camille Graf, Maud Langlois, Éric Thiébaut, Michel Tallon, Clémentine Béchet, Markus Feldt, Valentin Fonteneau, Clément Schotte
Items.Title: A comparative study between Zernike WFS and iMZ on the CRAL XAO test bench
Items.Abstract: The Mach-Zehnder wavefront sensor (WFS) and the Zernike WFS share many similarities, as they are both interferometric wavefront sensors that use a Fourier filtered reference wavefront. In the context of exoplanet detection with futur extremely larges telescopes, these sensors are potential candidates for second-stage adaptive optics systems. In this contribution, we analyse the similarities and differences between the ZWFS and the integrated Mach-Zehnder (iMZ) WFS, using simulated METIS first-stage residuals. We first report on our simulation results for different science cases under various turbulence and flux conditions. In a second step, we present recent experimental results obtained on the CRAL XAO test-bench. The first-stage residuals are generated with a 1024x1024 Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) and wavefront correction is performed with a deformable mirror with 24x24 actuators. Another SLM is used to create a reflective Zernike mask, with a diameter of approximatively 15 pixels.

Items.Authors: Mala Mateen, Denis W. Oesch
Items.Title: A comparative study of WFS performance to dynamic turbulence
Items.Abstract: Many current and future imaging systems on ground-based telescopes incorporate high sensitivity wavefront sensors like the non-linear Curvature wavefront sensor (nlCWFS) and the pyramid wavefront sensor (PWFS). These sensors effectively utilize the available photons to sense the lowest order modes that dominate atmospheric turbulence. These low order modes diffract light at small angular separations where an exo-planet may reside.  In the Starfire High-contrast ADaptive Optics Wavefront sensor (SHADOW) lab we have built an optics testbed equipped with an atmospheric turbulence simulator (ATS), and a modular adaptive optics system that can close the loop with a SHWFS, a PWFS, and an nlCWFS. We explore the fundamental limit of wavefront sensing for each sensor and map out the optimal performance regime for each wavefront sensor as a function of available photons, atmospheric parameters, and dynamic range.

Items.Authors: Adam Garner, David Copley, Iain Steele, Helen Jermak, Chloe Miossec, Graciela Delgado, Horacio Rodríguez
Items.Title: A control architecture overview of the New Robotic Telescope (NRT)
Items.Abstract: The New Robotic Telescope is a 4m fully autonomous telescope being built on la Palma by Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC) and University of Oviedo (UoO). This telescope is being designed with time domain astronomy in mind with a 30 second time to target allowing rapid follow up of targets of opportunity.   The telescope has many subsystems based on Beckhoff Twincat 3 PLCs. We provide an overview of each subsystem, the design choices that have been made and how the overall distributed control system architecture links each together using OPC UA protocol, including sharing safety systems and telemetry between them. We also provide our approach to prototyping and validating the subsystems currently in development, in particular, connection to the wider NRT software stack.

Items.Authors: Daiana Ribeiro Bortoletto, José Octavio Armani Paschoal, Rafael Alves de Souza Ribeiro, Cláudia Mendes de Oliveira, Laerte Sodré
Items.Title: A decade overview of the GMT-Brazil project
Items.Abstract: The GMT/FAPESP project, initiated in 2014 in Brazil, enabled the formation in 2015 of a highly qualified group, designated GMT Brazil Office, focused on the development of engineering projects in astronomical instrumentation, as well as innovation in management and auxiliary systems. The team, composed of more than 70 people, has a broad scope of work in various areas related to the GMT telescope, such as its participation in the development of GMT instrumentation projects; the generation of content and production of videos for scientific dissemination; the improvement and execution of advanced astronomy courses for high school teachers; the promotion of institutional relations and interaction with companies; and the development and improvement of management and governance systems. This article presents the team's trajectory in the GMT/FAPESP project, the management tools and processes developed, and the main results achieved in their areas of activity over the 10 years of the project.

Items.Authors: Braden Gail, Suresh Sivanandam, Saugata Dutt, Gavin Hay, Shaojie Chen, Patrick Nkwari, Shane Jacobson
Items.Title: A fiber-fed illumination technique for cryogenic quantum efficiency measurement and characterization of the HAWAII-4RG infrared detector
Items.Abstract: We present a new method for measuring the quantum efficiency (QE) of infrared detector arrays inside cryogenic, vacuum environments. Traditional optical calibration setups are challenging to implement in these conditions. To address this, we developed a fiber-optic illumination system that splits the monochromator output between a calibrated photodiode outside the cryostat and the detector under test inside. This design provides stable, well-controlled light delivery suitable for cryogenic instrumentation. Using this approach, we characterized the QE and key performance metrics of the Teledyne HAWAII-4RG infrared detector, including dark current, read noise, and persistence. These results establish a robust performance baseline for future instrument integration and offer a generalizable framework for precision detector calibration in cryogenic systems.

Items.Authors: Hugo Gaquere, Damien Gratadour, Cyril Tasse, Olivier Aumage
Items.Title: A high-performance GPU accelerated modular framework for radio-interferometric deconvolution
Items.Abstract: Deconvolution in modern radio-interferometric imaging pipelines face severe performance constraints: deconvolution represents a bottleneck and current implementations lack of portability. We propose a modular GPU-accelerated framework for radio-astronomy deconvolution, to improve runtime performance, portability across pipelines and to reduce algorithm implementation overhead.

Items.Authors: Yilong Ma, Wei Gao, Chao Shen, Fengtao Wang, Wei Li, Wei Xin, Zongxi Song, Hongju Zhang
Items.Title: A high-precision, low-noise camera for transiting photometry based on CMOS sensor stitching with high stability of gain
Items.Abstract: The research team carried out the development and performance evaluation of a low-noise, high gain-stability camera for transiting photometry. With China's independently developed CMOS sensors as its cores and in response to the needs of high-precision photometry, the camera adopts a multi-sensor stitching scheme with techniques such as low-noise power supplies, vacuum cooling, precise assembly and alignment. Particularly, it has achieved a high stability of gain by optimizing the gain bias circuit and applying a high-precision temperature control for the sensors. With a high-precision photometric platform, the research team conducted long-term observations of a 12.5-magnitude star with the camera. The results show that both the readout noise and dark current are controlled at expected low levels. The camera’s photometric precision enables effective detection of the varied weak light signals caused by transiting of Earth-sized planets.

Items.Authors: Gaston D. Baudat, Laurent Jolissaint, David Lavanchy, Jonathan Coelho, Guillaume Müller
Items.Title: A machine-learning approach to image-space wavefront sensing in adaptive optics
Items.Abstract: AI4Wave is an artificial-intelligence-based image-space wavefront sensing solution already used in optical alignment, surface testing, and metrology. It reconstructs the full wavefront from a single defocused image using a deterministic feed-forward neural network trained entirely on synthetic data. Requiring only a camera and imaging lens, AI4Wave eliminates lenslet arrays and their dynamic-range limits, operates from near-flat to multi-wavelength aberrations, and can measure several sources simultaneously in one image. In this work, AI4Wave is applied to adaptive optics (AO), where a NVIDIA Jetson-based implementation provides real-time phase retrieval for closed-loop control using an Alpao DM97 deformable mirror. Compact, alignment-friendly, and layout-independent, AI4Wave extends AI-driven wavefront sensing to real-time AO correction.

Items.Authors: Achrene Dyrek, Pierre-Olivier Lagage, Sarah Kendrew, Mael Voyer, Jeroen Bouwman, Michiel Min, Giuseppe Morello, Thomas Greene, Taylor Bell, Hannah Diamond-Lowe
Items.Title: A new window in time: a mid-infrared slit spectroscopy mode for precision time-series astronomy with JWST/MIRI
Items.Abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) delivers transformative mid-infrared sensitivity for time-series spectroscopy. A new effort is under way to test the performance and scientific potential of the MIRI Low Resolution Spectrometer in fixed-slit mode for time-series observations. Using the slit suppresses the thermal background that currently limits the precision of shallow signals - such as terrestrial exoplanets or faint stars - when using the slitless configuration. A dedicated fixed-slit subarray is also being developed, which could be used to reduce systematics associated with low frame counts in full-array readout mode. Newly acquired full-array calibration data allow direct slit–slitless performance comparisons, identifying regimes where the fixed-slit mode improves the signal-to-noise ratio. This presentation will detail the resulting instrument behavior, key performance gains, and recommended strategies for adopting this new mode once integrated on-board MIRI.

Items.Authors: Solange Ramírez, Jeffrey Crane, Alan Uomoto
Items.Title: A project management plan for mid-scale and small ground-based instrumentation projects
Items.Abstract: We describe a project management plan tailored for mid-scale and small instrumentation projects. The project management plan has been conceived to promote communication among team members, to use common tools, and to implement processes that are cost effective and appropriate for mid-scale to small projects. This plan has been developed to organize, plan, and control the instrumentation activities carried out by the technical team at the Carnegie Observatories and it has been applied to managing the preliminary design phase for the GMT Commissioning Camera and the Magellan Infrared Multi-Object Spectrograph (MIRMOS).

Items.Authors: William R. McBride, Jayadev Rajagopal, Emily Hunting
Items.Title: A Standardized PLC Modernization Paradigm for Observatory Upgrades Across NOIRLab Facilities
Items.Abstract: As telescopes age, maintaining telescope systems becomes increasingly difficult due to obsolescence and the decreasing reliability of control systems and electronics. In this paper, we propose modernizing telescope systems by replacing obsolete custom hardware with programmable logic controllers (PLCs). Unlike most off-the-shelf and custom computer-controlled systems, PLCs are reliable, easy to program and maintain, and have factory support for many decades. This upgrade approach improves longevity, reliability, and performance while simplifying maintenance and reducing reliance on legacy expertise. Additionally, a PLC system allows for enhanced maintenance and remote troubleshooting capabilities. The advantages of this approach include increased longevity of telescope subsystems, significantly enhanced reliability, lower maintenance costs, improved remote troubleshooting and support, and a cost-effective framework applicable to other telescopes and astronomical instruments.

Items.Authors: Ricardo Zanmar Sánchez, Salvatore Savarese, Vittorio Braga, Marcella Di Criscienzo, Giuliana Fiorentino, Pietro Schipani, Laura Schreiber, Joshua Meyers, Sandrine J. Thomas
Items.Title: A wavefront sensor method based on science image analysis: application to the Vera C. Rubin observatory
Items.Abstract: We present a wavefront sensor technique based on the analysis of elongation patterns of science star fields. Our method relies on a parametric model to calculate the wavefront error throughout the focal plane and we use it to analytically derive moments of stars. With numerical optimization we find the corresponding misalignments (rigid body and mirror deformations) that best reproduce a given ellipticity pattern of stars. In this work we apply the method to science images observed during the commissioning of the LSST of the Vera C. Rubin observatory and present some lessons learned and limitations of this technique.

Items.Authors: Nicolas Doucet, Damien Gratadour, Cyril Tasse
Items.Title: Accelerating facet based gridding with GPU
Items.Abstract: The SKA radio telescope project requires efficient processing of massive data volumes  We developed a GPU accelerated Baseline Dependent Averaging gridder capable of handling Direction Dependent Effects, including Jones matrices. That implementation is integrated into DDFacet for full pipeline testing and comparison.

Items.Authors: Daniel Lancaster, Stefan Kraus, Sorabh Chhabra, Owain Snaith, Jyotirmay Paul
Items.Title: Acceptance testing of the CRED ONE camera for BIFROST
Items.Abstract: BIFROST is soon to be part of the ASGARD visitor suite of instruments for the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI). BIFROST will have two spectrographs that can be used together for fringe tracking and for different spectral resolutions. Both spectrographs will be equipped with their own First Light Imaging CRED ONE NIR camera. The design and implementation of these two cameras is different to that of a normal CRED ONE. The camera is designed for ultra-low noise and a slower acquisition rate. To achieve this, the cold-stop aperture of the system is minimised to still accept the beam of BIFROST but minimise background light. In this paper we will discuss the acceptance testing preformed in December 2024 and follow up testing later in the year. This will include acceptance F-number characterisation as well as sensor performance metrics.

Items.Authors: Michael J. Ireland, Frantz Martinache, Stefan Kraus, Denis Defrère, Peter Tuthill, Daniel Ahrer, Fatmé Allouche, Emilie Bouzerand, Julia Bryant, Joshua Carter, Sorabh Chhabra, Benjamin Courtney-Barrer, Fred Crous, Nick Cvetojevic, Daniel Dahl, Steve Ertel, Juan Pablo Gil, Adrian Glauser, Xavier Habois, Lucas Labadie, Stéphane Lagarde, Daniel Lancaster, Connor Langford, Romain Laugier, Roxanne Ligi, Grace McGinness, Marc-Antoine Martinod, Alexandra Mazzoli, Anthony Meilland, Kwinten Missiaen, Sébastien Morel, Barnaby Norris, Laurent Pallanca, Jyotirmay Paul, Romain Petrov, Nicholas Schuhler, Gert Raskin, Sylvie Robbe-Dubois, J. Gordon Robertson, Ahmed Sanny, Owain Snaith, Adam Taras
Items.Title: Achieving the highest angular resolution and contrast with Asgard instrumental suite for ESO’s VLTI: commissioning results and projected performance
Items.Abstract: Asgard is a suite of visitor instrument modules for the ESO’s Very Large Telescope Interferometer designed to deliver high-contrast interferometric capability at infrared wavelengths through the phased installation of adaptive-optics, fringe-tracking, spectroscopic, and nulling instrumentation. The full instrumental suite will deliver by far the highest spectral and spatial resolution in the southern hemisphere (1 milli-arcsec and R~25,000 in Y with BIFROST), while also enabling exoplanet characterisation at 4-milli-arcsec resolution and 105 contrast in the L’ band using Nott. The first phase (Heimdallr, Baldr and Solarstein) is commissioned, the second phase underway, and the third phase due for completion early 2027. We will report on design, commissioning performance and anticipated scientific reach of the full instrument suite.

Items.Authors: Jocelyn Ferrara
Items.Title: Adaptive beyond optics: scalable project assurance for diverse astronomical instrumentation programs
Items.Abstract: Programs at Caltech Optical Observatories span a wide range of technical complexity, stakeholder expectations, and budgets, making one-size-fits-all project assurance impractical for 5–30 m telescope instruments. With a single Systems Engineer responsible for end-to-end assurance, a scalable, efficient strategy was needed. We developed an adaptive framework that tailors industry and NASA standards, providing scalable plans for requirements, risk/hazard control, configuration management, QA, and EH&S. Accessible tools and templates enable all team members to integrate assurance into daily workflows. Implementation has improved requirements stability, documentation quality, and early identification of integration and safety hazards. This paper describes the framework, deployment lessons, and guidance for observatories seeking effective assurance under constrained resources.

Items.Authors: Andreas Sinn, Georg Schitter
Items.Title: Adaptive optics for small telescope systems in space debris observation and free-space optical communication
Items.Abstract: Small telescope systems are powerful tools for observation of space debris objects, as well as active satellites in low-Earth-orbit (LEO). Free-space optical (FSO) communication provides high-speed data transmission for downlink and global communication. The influence of atmospheric turbulence, vibrations and wind shake limits the achievable performance. An adaptive optics system addressing the requirements of both applications is implemented and evaluated on a horizontal link under severe turbulence. An improvement of the RMS wavefront error by a factor of 4.8 is achieved.

Items.Authors: Pierre Janin-Potiron, Morgan Gray, Benoît Neichel, Jean-François Sauvage, Cédric Taïssir Héritier, Pierre Jouve, Romain Fétick, Thierry Fusco, Maxime Dumont
Items.Title: Advancements in estimating differential pistons for the Extremely Large Telescope using deep learning : II. Exploiting defocused images
Items.Abstract: The optical performance of the ELT relies on the precise estimation and correction of differential pistons between the six petals that form the M4 mirror. In a previous study, we demonstrated that a residual network can effectively estimate the differential piston from 2×2 Shack–Hartmann (SH) images, using one trained network per subaperture.  We now extend this approach to a different sensing configuration using defocused images as input, recovering all five differential pistons from a single image. We evaluate the sensitivity of this sensor concept with respect to key variables (number of averaged frames, atmospheric turbulence strength, detector noise).  Furthermore, we exploit multi-wavelength measurements and show that feeding three wavelengths simultaneously to the network enhances the capture range with minimal modifications to the baseline architecture. Finally, preliminary results suggest that combining SH and defocused image data may further improve the robustness of the method

Items.Authors: Jill Juneau, Declan O'Neill, Peter Orel, Sven Herrmann, Gregory Prigozhin, Eric Miller, Robert Goeke, Elio Angilè, Mark Bautz, Steven Allen, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Kevan Donlon, Catherine E. Grant, Beverly LaMarr, Christopher Leitz, Glenn Morris, Abigail Y. Pan, Tonya Peshel, Haley Stueber, Keith Warner
Items.Title: Advancing the AXIS camera front-end electronics architecture through the AXIS-TAP technology platform
Items.Abstract: The Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS) will deliver arcsecond imaging in the soft X-ray band. Its High-Speed Camera employs four MIT Lincoln Laboratory CCDs that are read out by the Front-End Electronics, which provides precision clocking, digitization, and formatted telemetry output. A parallel technology maturation effort is advancing key subsystems using the AXIS Testing and Acquisition Platform (AXIS-TAP) designed as a flight-like FPGA/ADC system that digitizes CCD signals and transmits image data over Ethernet. AXIS-TAP integrates with the existing STA Archon readout to enable side-by-side performance testing. Results show equivalent or improved read noise and linearity, validating the architecture for integration into the AXIS flight electronics.

Items.Authors: Manjunath Bestha, Sonith L. S.
Items.Title: AI-Based Wavelength Calibration for Automated Pipelines
Items.Abstract: Wavelength calibration establishes a relationship between detector pixels and known wavelengths in a spectrographs, ensuring that the measured spectra correspond to their true physical wavelengths. In this work, we present an AI-based method for calibrating the wavelengths of ground-based, single-order, low-resolution spectrographs. The approach identifies line centroids, handles blended features, and tracks instrument drifts to produce stable pixel-to-wavelength solutions. Trained on both arc-lamp and on-sky frames, the method improves calibration repeatability and reduces frame-to-frame shifts in HFOSC–HCT data, while also decreasing processing time compared to traditional IRAF line-identification routines. As a long-term goal, this work explores the potential for autonomous AI systems to eventually replace manual or semi-manual pipeline development for spectroscopic data reduction.

Items.Authors: Jeffrey Crane, Suresh Sivanandam, Gavin Hay, André Anthony, Jenny Atwood, Mark Barnet, Shaojie Chen, Saugata Dutt, Olivier Lardière
Items.Title: Alignment and integration plan for the Gemini Infrared Multi-Object Spectrograph and imager
Items.Abstract: The Gemini Infrared Multi-Object Spectrograph and imager (GIRMOS) is the first science instrument planned to use the upcoming Gemini North Adaptive Optics (GNAO) system at the Gemini North Observatory. GIRMOS is a cryogenic instrument featuring four parallel spectrograph channels and a single parallel imaging channel. Each spectrograph channel is fed by an object selection system with integrated multi-object adaptive optics that operates in open loop behind GNAO. The alignment and integration plan ensures precise optical and mechanical alignment of all subsystems, so that all five observing channels are co-aligned and ready for testing and final verification.

Items.Authors: John G. Hagopian, Matthew Bolcar, Bente Eegholm, Tyler Groff, David Kubalak, Alice Liu, Catherine Marx, Kyle McClean, Greg Wenzel, Guangjun Gao
Items.Title: Alignment of the Roman Space Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Roman Space Telescope (Roman) is NASA’s next great Observatory scheduled to be launched in September of 2026. Roman will observe Exoplanets and dark energy and will advance topics ranging from galaxy evolution to the study of objects within the galaxy. Roman is comprised of a 2.4-m telescope with two relay channels, the Integrated Optical Assembly (IOA); a Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and a Coronagraph Instrument (CGI). An Instrument Carrier (IC) meters these payload elements to each other and to the spacecraft bus (S/C). These five elements comprise the Observatory and require precision alignment for optimal performance. This paper details the alignment plan, budget and processes used to ensure alignment of each element and of the integrated system to meet the pupil and wavefront error requirements. In addition, verification of alignment during thermal vacuum testing of the Spacecraft/Integrated Payload (SCIPA) level testing of the assembly is reported.

Items.Authors: Alexandra N. Higley, Randall McEntaffer, Bridget O'Meara, James Tutt, Jake McCoy, Ross McCurdy, Jeffrey De Lucca, Tristen Sextro, Aditi Gangadharan, Garrett Brady, Cooper Akers, Nathaniel Hamme, Alberto Moretti, Daniele Spiga, Stefano Basso, Vadim Burwitz, Gisela Hartner, Andreas Langmeier, Thomas Müller, Surangkhana Rukdee, Thomas Schmidt, Andrew Holland, Daniel Evan, Karen Holland, David Colebrook, David Gopinath, Max Collon, David Girou, Nicolas Barrière, Marc Verschuuren, Manuel Paans, Jeroen Haneveld, Mark Olde Riekerink, Bart Schurink, Casey DeRoo, Benjamin Donovan, William Zhang, Ryan McClelland, Kai-Wing Chan, Raul Riveros, Michael Biskach, Peter Solly, Timo Saha
Items.Title: An overview of the Off-plane Grating Rocket Experiment Pathfinder (OGRE-P)
Items.Abstract: The Off-plane Grating Rocket Experiment (OGRE) is a sounding rocket mission that is designed to demonstrate high-performance next-generation X-ray technology for soft X-ray spectroscopy. The nominal payload features a three-component spectrometer consisting of a modern X-ray mirror assembly, modules of blazed reflection gratings with radial groove profiles, and an array of electron-multiplying CCDs. While in flight, OGRE aims to obtain the highest resolution soft X-ray spectrum of Capella to date. As modern X-ray mirror technology continues to develop, the OGRE team will launch a pathfinder mission that uses an existing mirror assembly, JET-X, in preparation for the nominal flight. This preliminary flight, designated as Pathfinder OGRE (OGRE-P), will test the X-ray reflection gratings for high-resolution spectroscopy and provide critical information on the in-flight operation of OGRE payload systems. Here. we report on the current status of the OGRE-P payload.

Items.Authors: Jordan Raffard, Pierre Vermot, Damien Gratadour
Items.Title: Analysis of deep learning-based methods for denoising pyramid wavefront sensor
Items.Abstract: The Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) has made adaptive optics (AO) essential for ground-based observatories, enabling real-time correction of atmospheric distortions to sharpen astronomical images. Current AO systems rely on pyramid wavefront sensors (pyrWFS), which, despite their high sensitivity, suffer from noise-induced measurement errors—especially when observing faint stars. This degradation limits performance in low-light conditions.  To overcome this, we propose using deep learning to enhance AO control loops by developing neural networks to denoise pyrWFS measurements. We designed several models and integrated them in AO simulations. Evaluations showed significant improvements in Strehl Ratio (SR) and system stability, demonstrating that deep learning can boost AO reliability, even in challenging conditions.  This approach advances AO technology, enabling high-fidelity imaging of faint celestial objects and unlocking the full potential of next-generation telescopes like the ELT.

Items.Authors: Pia Knopp, Alexander Altmann, Norbert Meidinger, Thomas Bechteler, Rafael Strecker, Jonas Mügge, Valeria Antonelli, Vadim Burwitz, Peter Lechner, Robert Andritschke
Items.Title: Analysis of electronic crosstalk effects in a 19-cell silicon drift detector for the eXTP mission
Items.Abstract: The enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry mission (eXTP) aims to explore the state of ultra-dense matter under extreme conditions of gravity and magnetism. A primary instrument of the satellite is the Spectroscopic Focusing Array (SFA) made up of six X-ray focusing telescopes of which five carry a 19-cell Silicon Drift Detector (SDD) each.   The SFA has to meet the crucial requirements of high detector throughput (system deadtime less than 5 % at 1 Crab), high time resolution below 10 μs, and good spectral resolution (energy resolution at 6 keV better than 180 eV). Fast readout of the detector signals is done by three high time resolution spectroscopy (HTRS) ASICs. To improve the spectral resolution, it is important to minimize electronic crosstalk effects in the detector system.   This paper explores the origin of electronic crosstalk in the detector system caused by proximity of signal lines or during signal processing with the goal of optimizing system performance in the future.

Items.Authors: Lawrence S. Jones, Chris A. S. Parmenter, Boris van Griensven, Archie Monk, Matthew Clapp, Nick Waltham
Items.Title: Analysis of event detecting front end electronics for X-ray optimised CIS detectors
Items.Abstract: In this work the authors discuss the technical challenges of operating X-ray CMOS image sensors (CIS) with photon counting event detection algorithms incorporated within the front end electronics (FEE). Implementing event detection algorithms early in the signal chain mitigates many of the system design impacts resulting from the high output data rate of these large format (>1 k by 1 k pixels) and high framerate (>10 fps) detectors. However, the FEE is typically resource constrained and therefore incorporating additional computational hardware within this subsystem brings with it significant engineering challenges.  With reference to experimental data, the authors explore the challenges arising from FEE based event detection implementations. This work focusses on the trade-offs that require consideration of detector behaviours to ensure that the scientific performance of the host instrument is maintained whilst still realising the benefits of using CIS detectors in X-ray applications.

Items.Authors: Paolo Di Marcantonio, Eric H. C. Stempels, Valentina Alberti, Manuel Amate Plasencia, Veronica Baldini, Frédérique Baron, Philippe Berio, Joar G. Brynnel, Alexandre Cabral, Bruno Chazelas, Lise Christensen, Michael Debus, Christine Füßlein, Wolfgang Gaessler, Omar Gabella, Elena Gallo, Rory Gillespie, Enrico Giro, Yevgeniy Ivanisenko, Heidi Korhonen, Izan de Castro Leão, Alessandro Marconi, Piotr Masłowski, Manuel Monteiro, Enrico Pinna, Monica Rainer, Chiara Selmi, Francesca Sortino, Rossella Spiga, Andrea Tozzi, Bachar Wehbe, Alessio Zanutta, Jennifer Zimara
Items.Title: ANDES, the high resolution spectrograph for the ELT: insights and lessons from the preliminary design phase
Items.Abstract: The paper introduces the management approach adopted during the Preliminary Design Phase for ANDES, the ESO/ELT high-resolution spectrograph. ANDES’s technical and organizational complexity — stemming from multiple subsystems and a large international consortium - called for a staggered strategy in which the overall preliminary design review was broken down into a series of subsystem-level reviews. We present an in-depth analysis of the lessons learned from implementing this decentralized methodology, examining the advantages and disadvantages encountered and outlining key recommendations to streamline the upcoming project phases.

Items.Authors: Michel Lortholary, Nathan Leguay, Thibault Pichon, Bastien Reboul, Christophe Cara, Gregory Kaszubiak
Items.Title: ARIEL-AIRS Electrical Ground Support Equipment (EGSE): building a flexible hardware and software solution that could be used for future projects
Items.Abstract: The ARIEL space telescope (ESA) will study the atmosphere of hundreds of exoplanets through its infrared spectrometer, named AIRS developed by a French consortium of laboratories. To enable this development, CEA teams have worked on a flexible and reliable solution of EGSE.    The EGSE shall allow the full control and readout of the two acquisition chains of the instrument : communication with the AIRS Detector Control Unit (A-DCU), power supply, images and housekeeping data acquisition and their display in real time, data storage and log of all sent commands.    We have build five EGSEs fully integrated into movable racks that can easily follow AIRS on various testing environments.    The software is made of LabVIEW (NI) for the graphic interfaces and Python to build elaborated sequences of tests.  The modularity and parametrization of these EGSEs would enable to adapt the software to next missions which require the same needs.

Items.Authors: Thomas Mattheussen, Germain Garreau, Marc-Antoine Martinod, Romain Laugier, Muhammad Salman, Kwinten Missiaen, Peter Marley Chingaipe, Wannes Verstraeten, Gert Raskin, Simon Gross, Michael J. Ireland, Lucas Labadie, Ahmed Sanny, Johan Morren, Azzurra Bigioli, András P. Joó, Stephen J. Madden, Alexandra Mazzoli, György Medgyesi, Bart Vandenbussche, Denis Defrère
Items.Title: Asgard/NOTT: status of laboratory nulling performance
Items.Abstract: Asgard/NOTT will leverage recent VLTI/GRAVITY+ upgrades and integrated optics beam combiners in the mid-infrared to become the first long-baseline nulling interferometer to probe the promising L’ band (3.5-4.0 um). Its aim is to directly image young giants near the snowline of nearby main-sequence stars, combining the VLTI’s 130m-long effective baseline with the high-contrast capability of nulling to reach the required sensitivity. We aim to demonstrate the required nulling sensitivity and stability on the test bench at KU Leuven.     This presentation gives an overview of the current nulling performance, optimization efforts, and limiting factors. Following broadband self-calibrated null depth measurements of (1.14±0.01)×10^-3, we present the first dispersed null depths. The throughput up to the chip is expected to be >40% after optimization and >25% after injection into the chip. We conclude with an outlook on the remaining optimization milestones and the expected on-sky performance.

Items.Authors: Daniel Echeverri, Nemanja Jovanovic, Ashley Baker, Mitsuko Roberts, Yann Terrien, Reston Nash, Garreth Ruane, Ricardo Meneses, James Brugger, Cody Lammer, Dimitri Mawet, Robert Bertz
Items.Title: Assembly and characterization of the front-end instrument (FEI) subsystem of Keck/HISPEC
Items.Abstract: The High-Resolution Infrared Spectrometer for Exoplanet Characterization (HISPEC) is a diffraction-limited, single mode fiber-fed, near-infrared spectrograph for the Keck Observatory that will deliver R~100,000 spectra across the y-K bands simultaneously (0.98–2.5 μm). This paper covers the front-end instrument (FEI) subsystem, which injects adaptive-optics-corrected light into the fiber bundles. We present the as-built FEI design and laboratory results validating various elements and end-to-end performance. This includes the tracking system, the dual-bundle injection and PIAA-enabled coupling gains, and an update on the fiber-nulling mode. Finally, we outline the timeline toward FEI delivery to Keck ahead of full-instrument deployment in 2027.

Items.Authors: Daniel P. Violette, Regina Caputo, Adrien Laviron, Kavic Kumar, Zachary Metzler, Grant Sommer, Nicolas Striebig, Richard Leys, Ivan Peric, Manoj Jadhav, Bobae Kim, Jessica Metcalfe, Abhradeep Roy, Yusuke Suda, Yasushi Fukazawa, Norito Nakano
Items.Title: A-STEP: payload integration and launch status
Items.Abstract: A medium-energy (100 keV to 100 MeV) gamma-ray telescope capable of spectroscopy, imaging, and polarization will deepen our understanding of the most energetic astrophysical phenomena and processes. To enable science in this regime, low-power and tileable detector technologies must be developed while still maintaining high spatial and spectral resolution capabilities. AstroPix detectors are high voltage monolithic active pixel sensors (HV-MAPS) that couple the above properties with on-chip signal digitization. The AstroPix Sounding Rocket Technology Demonstration Payload (A-STEP) will be the first operating AstroPix detectors in a space environment and a step towards larger integrated AstroPix systems. A-STEP seeks to detect charged particle tracks in the ionosphere as they pass through a stack of three layered 2x2 AstroPix detector arrays. I will provide highlights from A-STEP’s calibration and integration campaign, along with updates on launch readiness and timeline.

Items.Authors: Peter P. Pedersen, David Degen, Lionel Garcia, Urs Schroffenegger, Sebastián Zúñiga-Fernández, Daniel Sebastian, Didier Queloz
Items.Title: Astra: A cross-platform, open-source, integrated, extensible observatory control software
Items.Abstract: We present Astra (Automated Survey observaTory Robotised with Alpaca), an open-source, cross-platform Python system for the sustained, fully autonomous operation of astronomical observatories.  Astra controls telescopes, cameras, domes, focusers, filter wheels, safety monitors, and weather sensors via the ASCOM Alpaca protocol and executes prescheduled observatory actions under continuous safety supervision, including advanced multi-device actions, such as plate-solve-based pointing correction using an offline Gaia–2MASS catalogue, PID-controlled autoguiding, and autofocusing.  A FastAPI web service provides a browser UI, REST and WebSocket APIs for real-time status, image previews, and SQLite-backed telemetry and logs. Currently, Astra is deployed at several professional facilities, including SPECULOOS-South (Chile), Saint-Ex (Mexico), and the ETH Observatory (Switzerland), delivering reliable, unattended survey operations.

Items.Authors: Hervé Geoffray
Items.Title: Athena X-IFU detection chain early demonstrations: recent results and implications for EM design
Items.Abstract: X-IFU instrument, the high-resolution X-ray spectrometer of the ESA Athena mission, will deliver spectra in the 0.2-12 keV range with a spectral resolution requirement of 4 eV up to 7 keV from 5" pixels, and a field of view of 4'. The detection chain is one of the major functional chains of the X-IFU instrument. CNES leads the project development for the X-IFU Consortium; partners of the main detection chain are NASA-GFSC, SRON, VTT, APC, NIST, IRAP, and IAP. Early demonstrations of the detection chain internal interfaces compatibility, functional validation and performances are a major step for the development plan. Warm electronics (WE) demonstrator models (DM) have been fabricated and tested, and coupled to the cold detection chain. Interconnect between the cold function and the WE drives the feasibility of the Time Domain Multiplexing used for the readout and have been extensively studied. This paper focuses on the results obtained on the DMs and the way forward for EM design.

Items.Authors: Marina Vela Nuñez, Alessio Pannocchia, Luca Serafini, Pierpaolo Merola, Mauro Focardi, Vladimiro Noce, Simone Chiarucci, Marianna Michelangnoli, Elisabetta Giani, Gianluca Marotta
Items.Title: Automated FFT verification framework for the ARIEL Instrument Control Unit Boot Software via TCL test sequences
Items.Abstract: The Boot Software (BSW) of space instruments is mission-critical, ensuring safe and reliable transition from power-on to operational state. This paper focuses on the BSW developed for the Instrument Control Unit (ICU) of the ARIEL payload of ESA’s M4 mission. An automated validation framework has been implemented to verify BSW functionalities via TCL test sequences, covering key services such as request verification, housekeeping, event reporting, memory and time management, connection tests, and on-board parameter management. The validation campaign has been executed on the Spacecraft Interface Simulator (SIS) and across multiple instrument models, with the current campaign performed on the ICU Engineering Model (EM). Results show improved repeatability, requirement coverage, early anomaly detection, and reduced manual effort, with methodology reusable for regression campaigns, Full Functional Tests (FFT), and future in-flight verification.

Items.Authors: Florian Quatresooz, Jérôme Henrion, Cyril Petit, Aurélie Bonnefois, Gaël Kermarrec, David Alaluf, Nicolas Védrenne
Items.Title: Automatic exploitation of adaptive optics telemetry for optical turbulence characterization and FSOC performance estimation
Items.Abstract: Characterization of atmospheric turbulence on free-space optical communication (FSOC) links is essential for optimizing FSOC performance and enabling mitigation approaches such as predictive adaptive optics. We developed a real-time turbulence-monitoring pipeline for FEELINGS, ONERA’s optical ground station near Toulouse (France), providing estimates of integrated turbulence parameters as well as Cn2 and wind profiles from the adaptive optics telemetry. We present turbulence statistics collected during GEO-satellite links in fall 2025 and show how these measurements inform FSOC performance metrics. Finally, we discuss extending this approach to other AO-equipped optical ground stations for network-wide turbulence sensing and performance prediction.

Items.Authors: Hui Kong, Jin Xu, Xiang Jiang, Ping Chen, Jialin Zhang
Items.Title: Automatic guide star simulation method and implementation based on the Mutian Telescope
Items.Abstract: This paper investigates the simulation and implementation of an automatic guiding method to address the tracking error issues of the Mutian Telescope caused by gear periodic errors, slight polar axis deviations, and structural gravity deformations. By establishing a tracking error model and developing a guiding simulation program, simulated star images containing PSF and noise were generated. A centroid extraction algorithm was used in conjunction with an error back-calculation model to construct a P/PI-controlled closed-loop algorithm, which outputs real-time correction commands for both axes. Simulations and preliminary experiments indicate that this method effectively suppresses star image trailing, improves tracking accuracy and star point stability, providing a reliable technical solution for high-precision observations with the Mutian Telescope.

Items.Authors: Cong Pan, Shihai Yang, Yun Li, Zhuangzhuang Deng, Yanpeng Guo, Jiajia Li, Penxu Fan
Items.Title: Azimuth bandwidth analysis of the 14.5-meter optical-infrared telescope
Items.Abstract: This paper focuses on the design of the azimuth-axis servo control system for a 14.5-meter optical-infrared telescope. A systematic analysis of control bandwidth is conducted, considering both mechanical structural dynamics and wind load disturbances. Based on system parameters and finite element analysis results, a two-mass spring-damping model is established as the core mechanistic representation. Using this model, the influence of mechanical resonance frequency on closed-loop control bandwidth, dynamic performance (overshoot, rise time, settling time), and steady-state error is thoroughly investigated. Results show that, while maintaining comparable dynamic performance, control bandwidth increases significantly with higher mechanical resonance frequencies. Under identical control parameters, increasing the resonance frequency effectively improves dynamic response, reducing overshoot and settling time.

Items.Authors: Aravind B. Valluvan, Steven E. Boggs, Andreas Zoglauer, Sophia Haight, Jarred Roberts, Albert Shih, John A. Tomsick
Items.Title: Benchmarking COSI’s in-flight activation background simulations using proton beam irradiation
Items.Abstract: The Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) is a gamma-ray space telescope launching in 2027 that is designed to survey the entire sky between 0.2 and 5 MeV. A major challenge in analyzing MeV data arises due to the strong, temporally-varying gamma-ray background produced by high-energy particles bombarding the spacecraft. Accurate estimation of the in-flight background spectrum is essential for both scientific analysis and predicting COSI’s observational sensitivity. To validate and refine existing Monte Carlo simulations of the background, we performed multiple controlled proton irradiations on a COSI detector, replicating key aspects of the space radiation environment. Here, we present benchmarking results comparing simulations with experimentally measured data, and demonstrate their impact on predicting COSI’s activation background and overall sensitivity.

Items.Authors: Summer Luo, Tiger Wang, Célia Blain, Delphine Barbon-Dubosc, Benoît Neichel, Tania Colaco, Julien Charton
Items.Title: Boosting instrument availability via early reliability analysis & simulation
Items.Abstract: Astronomical observatories increasingly demand high system availability to overcome the maintenance challenges of remote sites. This shift toward resilient, remotely operable instruments drives new reliability standards. This presentation outlines the challenges and strategies developed by Australian Astronomical Optics (AAO) to enhance instrument reliability and resilience.

Items.Authors: Arlene J. Aleman, Justin R. Crepp
Items.Title: Branch point tolerant reconstruction for the nonlinear curvature wavefront sensor
Items.Abstract: The nonlinear Curvature Wavefront Sensor (nlCWFS) achieves high sensitivity to phase and amplitude aberrations by measuring intensity in multiple defocused planes. Nevertheless, strong turbulence conditions present a challenging phase-retrieval problem for consistent wavefront recovery. The Gerchberg–Saxton (GS) algorithm is often used as the reconstruction engine in nlCWFS pipelines, due to its simplicity and compatibility with forward/backward Fresnel propagations, however GS has a tendency to stagnate in local minima and fail in the presence of branch points. To overcome these limitations, we are developing nonlinear least-squares (NLLS) methods as a robust alternative to the GS algorithm by directly minimizing the difference between measured and model-predicted multi-plane intensities. We present regularized, branch-point tolerant reconstruction algorithms that are strong candidates for next-generation phase retrieval pipelines.

Items.Authors: Louis C. Desdoigts, Sebstiaan Haffert, Laird Close, Jared Males, Maggie Kautz, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: Bridging the gap: high dynamic range piston-mode recovery and non-linear wavefront reconstruction algorithms using the HDFS
Items.Abstract: Segmented ELT pupils introduce large differential piston modes that standard wavefront sensors cannot track. The Holographic Dispersed Fringe Sensor (HDFS) addresses this by converting segment pairs into spectrally dispersed interferometers with multi-wave capture range. We present efficient linear piston-recovery algorithms operating in the Fourier domain, where the differential piston signal becomes linear and resilient to residual aberrations. We then extend the approach using a differentiable forward model of the HDFS to perform non-linear wavefront reconstruction, recovering low-order modes not well suited for purely inverse methods. Together these methods establish a unified, high-dynamic-range reconstruction framework suitable for ELT phasing and future telemetry-driven wavefront control architectures.

Items.Authors: Daniele Spiga, Giorgia Sironi, Alberto Moretti, Desiree Della Monica Ferreira, Arne 'S Jegers, Marcos Bavdaz, Matteo Guainazzi, Erik Kuulkers
Items.Title: Building an analytical simulation tool for the effective area and the stray light of NewAthena
Items.Abstract: NewAthena, the largest X-ray telescope ever built with a launch scheduled near 2037, will be based on the technology of Silicon Pore Optics (SPO). Due to the intrinsic complexity of the SPO, and the number of obstructions that may occur when X-rays propagate throughout the optics structure, a simulation tool for the effective area and the stray-light impact due to off-axis sources is essential to determine the concentration power, the field of view, and the background level in the detector area. In the context of the ESA-supported SIMPOSIUM project, we have developed a fast software tool based on the implementation of an analytical algorithm, and validate the results by means of the SPORT ray-tracing tool. We show the expected results in terms of effective area and stray-light contamination of the field of view.

Items.Authors: Hugo Rousset, Manon Lizzana, Sébastien Soler, Fabrice Pancher, Julien Michelot, Logi Olgeirsson, Jean Baptiste Le Bouquin, Fabien Malbet
Items.Title: Calibration of pixel grid location of a CMOS silicon matrix detector based on Young’s fringes for space-based high accuracy astrometry
Items.Abstract: In the context of exoplanet detection an hosted payload on the future NASA's HWO has been proposed. The purpose of this proposal is to detect Earth-like planets at distances of up to 10 parsecs using the star's astrometric signal. In order to detect this signal, the centroid of the star must be measured at sub-microarcsecond precision. The preliminary error budget necessitates a pixel position knowledge requirement on the focal plane geometry of down to 5e-5pix. Researchers have been working on a calibration method based on the projection of scrolling Young's fringes on a matricial detector. This method is used to measure the geometrical shift of the pixel's peak response. The present study involves the simulation of the aforementioned calibration method and sensitivities to instrumentation instabilities. Subsequently, the positional coordinates of the initial pixel were determined through the utilisation of a dedicated testbed that was derived from the work of (Crouzier, 2016).

Items.Authors: Dominique Heinis, Joan Torras Estruch, Alejandro Sánchez, Antonio Carballedo, Giuseppe Vacanti, David Girou, Marcos Bavdaz
Items.Title: Calibration of the Minerva beamline for the characterization of the mirror modules of the NewAthena space telescope
Items.Abstract: The Minerva Beamline at the ALBA synchrotron is a dedicated metrology facility operating at the soft X-ray energy range (1 keV) used to support the development, testing, and fabrication of the optics for the upcoming NewAthena X-ray space observatory, an European Space Agency (ESA) L-class mission, planned to be adopted in 2027. The building block units of the telelescope optics are the mirror modules (MM), based on the Sillicon Pore Optics (SPO) technology, initially developed by cosine company in cooperation with ESA. In this work we will provide an overview of the beamline elements and the calibration performed in the beamline required for the characterization of the MMs. Recent results on the beamline performance in terms of repeatability and stability in the characterization of the MM will be discussed.
